title: India Crossed 150 GW of Solar Power. Then It Had to Switch Off a Sixth of It.
excerpt: The country added a record 44.6 GW in a single year and became the world's third-largest solar market. But the grid cannot absorb what the panels produce, and the paradox is getting worse.
body:
India's solar story has a plot twist nobody planned for. The country crossed the 150 GW milestone of installed solar capacity in March 2026, adding a record 44.6 GW in a single financial year — nearly doubling the previous year's 23.8 GW. It now ranks third globally in renewable energy capacity, behind only China and the United States. By annual installations, it is on track to become the world's second-largest solar market this year.

But on May 1, operators were forced to switch off 27.3 GW of solar capacity — roughly one-sixth of the country's entire installed base. On May 31, another 19.5 GW was curtailed. Electricity prices on the Indian Energy Exchange hit zero. And state governments, faced with the irony of too much clean power, are signing new coal deals.

## The Curtailment Crisis

Curtailment — forcibly reducing solar generation to protect grid stability — is not new. But the scale is. In a single day in May, 121.5 GWh of solar energy was wasted, more than many mid-sized countries produce in a week. Between May and December 2025, total curtailment was 2,300 GWh. The May 2026 numbers suggest 2026 will dwarf that figure.

"Instances of curtailment of 50 GWh or 100 GWh in a day are significant," said Duttatreya Das, energy analyst at Ember. The problem is structural: India's grid was built for a coal-dominated system where supply is constant and controllable. Solar output peaks at midday and drops to zero at sunset, creating a daily cycle of surplus and deficit that the grid's infrastructure cannot smooth.

The transmission network — particularly in solar-heavy states like Rajasthan, Gujarat, and Maharashtra, which together account for nearly 80% of new capacity — has not expanded fast enough to move power to where it is needed. Rajasthan alone added 12.1 GW of solar in FY2026, but its transmission corridors are saturated.

## The Numbers Behind the Milestone

The raw achievement is still remarkable. India reached its first 50 GW of solar in 11 years. The next 50 GW took three years. The most recent 50 GW took just 14 months.

Rooftop solar crossed 25 GW, driven by the PM Surya Ghar scheme that has covered 2.6 million homes with ₹14,771 crore ($1.8 billion) in central assistance. Wind power also hit a record with 6.05 GW added — the highest since 2016-17. Total renewable capacity, including large hydro, reached 283.5 GW, forming 51% of India's installed power base for the first time.

The National Solar Energy Federation of India (NSEFI) projects India will need 280-300 GW of solar by 2030 to meet its 500 GW non-fossil capacity target. At current rates of addition — approaching 50 GW annually — the generation target is achievable. The question is whether the grid can keep up.

## Distribution Companies in Distress

The crisis is compounded by the behaviour of state distribution companies (discoms). Facing surplus solar during peak generation hours, discoms have been dumping power on electricity exchanges at below cost. Spot prices crashing to zero does not help renewable investors who signed power purchase agreements at ₹2-3 per unit — they still get paid, but the discoms absorb the loss, deepening their already precarious financial position.

Meanwhile, the same discoms are contracting new thermal capacity for evening and night hours when solar drops off. The result is a system that is simultaneously overbuilt for midday and underbuilt for evening — a planning failure that battery storage could solve but has not yet arrived at scale.

## What Would Fix It

The fix is known but expensive: grid-scale battery storage, expanded interstate transmission, and smart grid management. India's battery storage pipeline stands at about 43 GW under various stages of bidding and development, but actual deployed capacity remains negligible. A 4-hour battery system at scale costs roughly ₹5-6 crore per MWh — manageable at policy level but requiring the kind of upfront capital that cash-strapped discoms cannot provide.

Pump-hydro storage — using surplus solar to pump water uphill during the day and releasing it through turbines at night — is also in the pipeline, with several projects in the Himalayas and Western Ghats. But these are five to seven-year projects, and the curtailment problem is here now.

For NRIs with investments in Indian renewable energy funds or companies, the paradox is a material risk. The sector's growth is not in question — India will almost certainly hit 300 GW of solar before 2030. But if a sixth of that capacity sits idle on any given day, the return profile of the underlying assets changes fundamentally. The infrastructure deficit is not a footnote to India's clean energy story. It is the story.

*Sources: Livemint; The Hindu BusinessLine; Construction World; JMK Research; PV Magazine; SolarQuarter; National Solar Energy Federation of India*
